newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage impasse spills over into New Year.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage impasse spills over into New Year.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori ignored a call for further talks from Marxist rebels holding 81 hostages in Lima, as the two week-old standoff spilled over into the New Year.
Fujimori, who has maintained a "no-concessions" stand throughout the crisis, refused to grab a double-edged sword offered him by guerrilla leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.
Cerpa told Fujimori on Tuesday "the doors of the residence are open" for government negotiator Domingo Palermo but insisted on the release of all the rebels' roughly 400 jailed comrades.
Earlier in the week Fujimori and his Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi said they hoped the standoff would be settled peacefully.

But on Wednesday Fujimori holed himself up in Government Palace and kept Palermo away from the compound. He was apparently angered by the rebels' publicity coup on Tuesday when Cerpa invited journalists inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.
Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed the residence in a hail of bullets during a reception on Dec. 17 in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito

Under an accord hashed out by the Red Cross, the two sides agreed journalists could cross police lines on Tuesday to film the residence close up. But the rebel leader summoned them inside the booby-trapped and mined compound.
Dressed in green military fatigues and covering his face with a red-and-white bandanna, Cerpa held court for about two hours as the rebels harangued Fujimori's "dictatorship."
"We are inflexible in our original position ... I do not see an immediate solution," Cerpa said.
While Fujimori refrained from sending a message to the hostages, Emperor Akihito spoke obliquely of the crisis.
"My heart hurts deeply when I think of those who cannot celebrate the New Year with their families," Akihito was quoted as saying by Japanese daily Yomiuri Shimbun.

Journalists who entered the Japanese compound on Tuesday described a scene like a ghost ship in the gardens of the residence. Empty bottles and discarded plates gave the residence the ironic appearance of many other post-New Year's Eve homes after Peru tried to celebrate the start of 1997.
Wary of alarming the 20-odd heavily armed rebels, however, Lima authorities had banned the usual cacophonous celebration of the New Year with rockets and fireworks in the San Isidro neighbourhood.

Reporters and police camped outside the residence twirled a few desultory sparklers at midnight but otherwise only the occasional explosion lit up the sky, and nothing that the rebels could interpret as an armed assault.
In the morning the subdued New Year's Eve melted into one more day in captivity for the top Peruvian officials, foreign diplomats and Japanese businessmen held under the guns by their MRTA captors.

As a sign of their continuing light mood inside, Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani kept up his series of visits to the compound bearing two guitars as accompaniment for the captives' now regular singing sessions.
With the gradual release of 420 hostages, the overcrowded conditions inside the two-storey mansion in the first week of the crisis have given way to a more relaxed atmosphere.
